name: Bezafibrate
lead: Bezafibrate is an oral fibrate lipid-lowering drug sold under brand names such as Bezalip. It lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL cholesterol, and it is described as a pan-agonist of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), acting on the alpha, gamma and delta subtypes.[1][2]

In fat-loss and looksmaxxing conversations it appears as a PPAR agonist that sits in the same receptor family as PPAR-delta compounds, which people discuss in connection with fat metabolism and leanness. The chain people have in mind runs from PPAR activation, to changes in how the body handles fats and glucose, to a leaner physique. Its documented uses, however, are medical: dyslipidemia, and off-label use in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC).[1][2][6]

It is a prescription medicine in the UK and the US.[1] Human trials have examined it in coronary artery disease, mixed dyslipidemia, PBC, cholestatic itch and several rare metabolic conditions.[4][5][8][9]

chain: Activates PPAR-alpha (and to a lesser degree gamma and delta)
Increases triglyceride clearance and fatty-acid handling
Discussed as a route toward leaner body composition
angle.text: People who discuss bezafibrate for body composition point to its pan-PPAR activity and its effect on triglycerides and glucose handling. Its published trial record concerns blood lipids and liver disease rather than appearance outcomes.

paras: Bezafibrate is used for combined hyperlipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia.[1][2] In Europe it is labelled for primary hyperlipidemias (Fredrickson types IIa, IIb, III, IV and V) and for secondary dyslipidemias when diet alone has not controlled lipid levels, according to Grokipedia's summary of the European indications.[2] It is generally regarded as a second-line fibrate option alongside fenofibrate and gemfibrozil.[2]

Wikipedia reports that its cardiovascular benefit appears mainly in patients with features of metabolic syndrome, and that studies suggest it may delay progression to diabetes in people with impaired glucose tolerance and slow worsening of insulin resistance. A prospective observational study cited there reported reductions in HbA1c regardless of concurrent antidiabetic medication.[1]

In primary biliary cholangitis, an autoimmune cholestatic liver disease that mainly affects middle-aged women, first-line therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid. A 2020 Lancet review describes off-label use of the pan-PPAR agonist bezafibrate as a recognised alternative for people who respond inadequately, alongside the licensed add-on obeticholic acid.[6] Newer reviews describe PPAR-pathway agents as the likely future of PBC treatment, including seladelpar and elafibranor.[3][4]

PPAR-delta agonists have attracted attention in fat-loss communities because the receptor is involved in fatty-acid oxidation in muscle. Bezafibrate enters that discussion as a marketed drug with partial PPAR-delta activity. No published human trial has measured fat mass, muscle mass or other appearance outcomes with bezafibrate as the primary goal.

Within the body-composition conversation, the chain people describe is indirect: PPAR activation raises fatty-acid oxidation and triglyceride clearance, which is associated with a more favourable lipid and glucose profile, and some users hope this translates into a leaner physique. The drug's own trial literature measures lipids, liver enzymes and clinical events rather than body fat or muscle, so what it does to appearance in healthy people has not been documented in published trials.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that the main toxicity is liver-related enzyme abnormalities, with myopathy reported and rhabdomyolysis rare.[1] Grokipedia lists gastrointestinal upset, a raised gallstone risk, and caution in renal impairment and in combination with statins; it describes the drug as contraindicated in severe hepatic or renal impairment, gallstone disease and pregnancy.[2]
Case reports include bezafibrate-associated neutropenia.[11] Product guidance calls for monitoring liver enzymes and kidney function, and dose adjustment in reduced kidney function.[2]

Like other fibrates, bezafibrate activates PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase activity and triglyceride clearance and raises apolipoprotein A-I and A-II; it also engages PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta to varying degrees, which is the basis for the term pan-agonist.[1][2] The wider effects attributed to it include improved insulin sensitivity, lower fibrinogen and reduced platelet aggregation.[2]
A mouse study found that PPAR-induced fatty-acid oxidation in T cells increased tumour-reactive CD8+ T cells and enhanced anti-PD-1 therapy, with bezafibrate used as the PPAR agonist.[12]

The three PPAR subtypes have distinct tissue roles. PPAR-alpha is highly expressed in liver, heart and skeletal muscle and governs fatty-acid uptake and beta-oxidation; PPAR-gamma is central to adipocyte differentiation and insulin sensitivity; PPAR-delta is prominent in skeletal muscle and drives fatty-acid oxidation. Bezafibrate's activity across all three, rather than predominantly alpha as with fenofibrate, is the reason researchers describe it as a pan-agonist and the reason it is studied in conditions of impaired fatty-acid oxidation.[1][2][15]
Grokipedia describes near-complete oral absorption and a plasma half-life of roughly 1-2 hours, with a sustained-release 400 mg formulation developed for once-daily use.[2]
Bezafibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative related to clofibrate, with the molecular formula C19H20ClNO4 and a molar mass of 361.82 g/mol.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes a synthesis in which the p-chlorobenzamide of tyramine undergoes a Williamson ether reaction with ethyl 2-bromo-2-methylpropionate, followed by hydrolysis of the ester to give the free acid.[1]

Wikipedia reports that bezafibrate was patented in 1971, introduced by Boehringer Mannheim in 1977, and approved for medical use in 1978; its sources give slightly different years.[1] Grokipedia states that it has been approved in the European Union since 1977 and that in the United States it lacks general approval but has received orphan designation for investigational use in PBC.[2]

Bezafibrate is a prescription-only drug in the UK and US.[1] Its profile in appearance-oriented forums is small and derives from its association with PPAR-delta compounds rather than from direct use reports. Pharmaceutical residues of bezafibrate are also tracked in environmental studies of wastewater treatment.[7]

The UK National Health Service lists bezafibrate as a prescription-only lipid regulator. In the United States, fenofibrate and gemfibrozil are the fibrates on the market, so bezafibrate is not routinely prescribed there outside investigational use.[1][2]

Small trials have been registered for bezafibrate in mitochondrial myopathy, fatty acid oxidation defects, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and bipolar depression.[13][14][15][16] In mice carrying a human tau mutation it reduced tau hyperphosphorylation, per Wikipedia. Wikipedia also notes a combination with chenodeoxycholic acid developed for hepatitis C, and preliminary University of Birmingham work on a combination with medroxyprogesterone acetate in cancer.[1]

The Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention (BIP) trial randomised 3,090 patients with previous myocardial infarction or stable angina and low HDL and/or high triglycerides, to test secondary prevention by raising HDL and lowering triglycerides.[9] Grokipedia summarises its results as a 9.4% relative reduction in the primary endpoint overall, with larger reductions in patients with metabolic syndrome features.[2]

A 2018 New England Journal of Medicine phase 3 trial (24 months, double-blind, placebo-controlled) randomly assigned 100 patients with PBC who had an inadequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid to bezafibrate or placebo added to standard therapy.[5] The FITCH trial, a randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 study, tested bezafibrate for itch in primary and secondary sclerosing cholangitis and PBC.[8] Earlier randomised work examined bezafibrate in PBC in 2003.[10]

Other human studies include a trial of bezafibrate in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy,[17] and registered studies in mixed dyslipidemia with berberine, hyperfibrinogenemia in acute myocardial infarction, cholestatic itch and mitochondrial myopathy.[18][19][13][14] No studies found examining bezafibrate for body-composition or appearance goals.

In the BIP trial the overall difference in the primary endpoint between bezafibrate and placebo was modest, and the authors reported larger reductions in patients with high baseline triglycerides, which is the origin of the observation that benefit clusters in people with metabolic-syndrome features.[9][2]

The 2018 NEJM trial in primary biliary cholangitis, conducted in France, reported that a substantially greater proportion of patients on bezafibrate than on placebo reached a normal composite biochemical liver profile at 24 months, and that the drug also improved itch and some fibrosis markers; elevations in creatinine were among the noted adverse findings.[5] The FITCH trial examined itch as the primary outcome across fibrosing cholestatic conditions.[8] Both studies enrolled patients with liver disease; neither was designed to assess body composition.

card.summary: A prescription fibrate and pan-PPAR agonist for blood lipids, discussed in fat-loss circles only by association with PPAR-delta compounds.
card.note: Established lipid drug; no studies of body-composition or appearance effects were found.

quick.overview:
Bezafibrate is a long-established prescription drug for high triglycerides and mixed cholesterol problems. It activates PPAR receptors, which is why it comes up alongside PPAR-delta compounds in fat-loss conversations.

Its trial record is in cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia and the liver condition primary biliary cholangitis. No trials of fat loss or appearance outcomes were found.
quick.mechanism: It activates PPAR-alpha mainly, with some activity at PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta, increasing triglyceride breakdown and altering HDL metabolism.
quick.risks: Reported effects include abnormal liver enzymes, muscle problems (rarely severe) and gastrointestinal upset. Sources list it as contraindicated in severe liver or kidney impairment, gallstone disease and pregnancy. It is prescription-only.
